## Overview

These papers apply Double Machine Learning (DML) and related debiased inference methods to estimate causal effects while controlling for high-dimensional confounders. The four papers showcase different DML variants: standard DML with heterogeneity analysis, DML adapted for a specific epidemiological design, DML for demand estimation, and Post-Double-Selection LASSO for variable selection in experimental reanalysis.

Expert groups may propose an alternative paper if they find one that better fits their interests. **Requirements:**

1. The paper must apply the unit's method
2. Health economics or health policy focus preferred
3. Submit the paper to Dr. Sylvia **by the Friday before the session** for approval
4. All group members must agree on the alternative paper

If approved, your group reads and presents the alternative paper instead of the assigned one.

## Paper 1: DML for Programme Evaluation

**Citation:** Knaus, M. C. (2022). Double machine learning-based programme evaluation under unconfoundedness. *The Econometrics Journal*, 25(3), 602-627.

**Why this paper?** This paper provides practical guidance on implementing DML for program evaluation, with an application to active labor market policies. It goes beyond average effects to explore *who benefits most* from treatment.

**Key methodological features:**

- Standard DML with cross-fitting
- Group Average Treatment Effects (GATEs)
- Best Linear Predictor of CATE
- Inference and confidence intervals for heterogeneous effects

[Access via UNC Libraries](https://academic.oup.com/ectj/article/25/3/602/6604901)

---

## Paper 2: DML for Vaccine Effectiveness

**Citation:** Jiang, C., et al. (2025). A double machine learning approach for the evaluation of COVID-19 vaccine effectiveness under the test-negative design. *Statistics in Medicine*. DOI: 10.1002/sim.70025.

**Why this paper?** This paper adapts DML to a specific epidemiological study design (test-negative design) used to evaluate COVID-19 vaccine effectiveness. It demonstrates how DML can improve causal inference in public health surveillance data with many potential confounders.

**Key methodological features:**

- DML-based doubly robust estimator (TNDDR)
- Adaptation of cross-fitting to test-negative design
- ML for nuisance functions in administrative health data
- Comparison with traditional regression approaches

[Access via PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39985144/)

---

## Paper 3: DML for Labor Supply Elasticities

**Citation:** Dube, A., Jacobs, J., Naidu, S., & Suri, S. (2020). Monopsony in online labor markets. *American Economic Review: Insights*, 2(1), 33-46.

**Why this paper?** This paper uses DML to estimate labor supply elasticities in online labor markets, demonstrating how DML handles high-dimensional controls in a clean empirical application. The economic mechanisms (monopsony power, wage-setting) parallel health economics questions about provider market power.

**Key methodological features:**

- DML for demand/supply estimation
- High-dimensional controls with LASSO first stage
- Application to platform economics
- Clean identification with rich behavioral data

[Access via AEA](https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aeri.20180150)

---

## Paper 4: Post-Double-Selection LASSO in Field Experiments

**Citation:** Cilliers, J., Elashmawy, A., & McKenzie, D. (2024). Using post-double selection LASSO to sharpen treatment effects in randomized experiments. World Bank Policy Research Working Paper #10931.

**Why this paper?** This paper meta-evaluates Post-Double-Selection LASSO (PDS-LASSO) across 36 randomized experiments, showing when and how this DML-related method improves precision. It provides practical guidance on when high-dimensional covariate adjustment helps (and when it doesn't).

**Key methodological features:**

- Post-Double-Selection LASSO (Belloni, Chernozhukov, Hansen 2014)
- Meta-evaluation across 36 RCTs
- Comparison: PDS-LASSO vs. standard OLS vs. ANCOVA
- Guidance on when high-dimensional adjustment improves precision

[Access via World Bank](https://documents.worldbank.org/en/publication/documents-reports/documentdetail/099536410112433490)

## Supplemental Reading

::: {.callout-note}
## Recommended Background

**D'Amour, A., Ding, P., Feller, A., Lei, L., & Sekhon, J. (2021).** Overlap in observational studies with high-dimensional covariates. *Journal of Econometrics*, 221(2), 644-654.

This paper highlights a critical challenge for DML: overlap violations become more severe as the number of covariates grows. Understanding when the positivity assumption fails is essential for interpreting DML results. [Access via UNC Libraries](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304407620303560)
:::

---

## Reading Tips

For each paper, focus on:

1. **The DML recipe:** How do they implement cross-fitting and debiasing?
2. **ML method choices:** Which learners do they use for nuisance functions?
3. **Variant differences:** How does this paper's DML variant differ from the others?
4. **Practical guidance:** What implementation advice does the paper offer?

Remember: DML doesn't solve the fundamental identification problem---it just handles high-dimensional nuisance parameters better than traditional methods.
